opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think about it in terms of how a human actually learns from a textbook versus how these models learn. Pre-training is kind of like skimming the textbook really, really fast, billions of times over. The model just reads the text and predicts the next token. That's an incredibly inefficient way to learn. If I just flipped through a dense math textbook once without engaging with it, I wouldn't come away understanding much.

What a person actually does is read a chapter, think about it, talk it over with a study partner, try the practice problems, get some wrong, go back and figure out why, and slowly build up real understanding. Right now the models basically don't do that. There's nothing analogous to working through the problems and digesting the material.

So the direction I'm excited about is some combination of self-play, synthetic data, and RL, where the model generates its own attempts, checks them, reflects on them, and learns from that loop. That's much more like how humans learn. And there's a strong reason to think it could be dramatically more sample-efficient, because you're squeezing far more learning out of each bit of data rather than just compressing the whole internet.

This also matters because of the data wall. We're running out of high-quality internet text, so the naive "just pre-train on more tokens" approach eventually runs into a ceiling. Whoever cracks this, getting models to learn more like a student with a textbook, unlocks a lot more scaling headroom. It's one of the big open research questions, and it's also why I think algorithmic secrets around this stuff are going to be so important going forward. The labs that figure it out could pull way ahead.

And it connects to what I'd call unhobbling more broadly. Today's models are capable but held back in silly ways: they can't really think for a long time, can't iterate, can't use their own outputs to get better. Once you let them do the equivalent of working on a problem for hours or days, checking their own work, learning from mistakes, I think you get a big jump in effective capability that isn't captured by just looking at pre-training compute curves.

r001.rationale: It contrasts passive next-token pre-training with actively working through problems, checking mistakes, and building understanding.

r002.rationale: It says the proposed self-play, synthetic-data, and RL loop could be more sample-efficient, but does not state that in-context learning is more sample-efficient than pre-training.

r003.rationale: It mentions RL as part of a learning loop, but does not characterize RL as distilling in-context learning into the model’s weights.

r004.rationale: It describes models learning from their own attempts, but does not compare those attempts as learning data with demonstrations of someone else’s solutions or explain why they are better.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing to recognize is just how inefficient pre-training actually is as a way of learning. You take trillions of tokens of internet text, and the model is basically learning by osmosis. It's reading everything, it's sort of soaking it in, but it's not really thinking about any of it. Compare that to how a human learns something hard. You read a textbook chapter, you stop, you try the problems, you get them wrong, you go back, you figure out where your mental model was off, you talk to a friend about it, you try to reproduce the derivation yourself. That loop is what actually produces understanding, and the current models mostly don't get to do that during training.

So the thing I find really exciting is what you might call the unhobbling of learning itself. Right now, if you look at the frontier models, they're in some sense incredibly knowledgeable but they're frozen. They learned a bunch of stuff once, and then they get deployed and they don't improve from the experience. A human intern who shows up at a company is not that useful on day one, but after six months they've absorbed the context, they've made mistakes and corrected them, they've built up intuitions about the specific problems. The models can't do that yet, and that's a huge handicap.

What I think changes this is a few things coming together. One is just RL on real tasks, where the model gets to try things, get feedback from the environment, and update. That's already a big part of why the reasoning models got so much better at math and code so fast. The feedback signal is clean, you can verify the answer, and the model learns from its own attempts rather than from imitating text. The second is something like self-play or synthetic data, where the model generates its own problems, its own critiques, its own training data, and the quality of that data can be much higher than random internet text because it's targeted at exactly the places where the model is weak. And then the third piece, which I think is the one people underrate, is continual learning. Letting the model actually carry forward what it figured out, so the learning compounds across episodes instead of being thrown away.

If you put those together, I think you get something that looks much more like how a scientist learns than how a language model has historically learned. And the reason that matters for the big picture is that it's the thing that lets you get past the data wall. We're running out of high-quality internet text, and if the only lever was scaling pre-training, that would be a real constraint. But if the model can learn from its own reasoning and its own experience, the bottleneck shifts from how much text exists to how much compute you can throw at letting the model think. And compute is something we know how to scale.

r001.rationale: Contrasts pre-training’s passive “learning by osmosis” from internet text with actively trying problems, correcting mistakes, and reproducing derivations.

r002.rationale: Does not state that in-context learning is more sample efficient than pre-training.

r003.rationale: Describes RL feedback and learning from attempts, but does not characterize RL as distilling in-context learning into the model’s weights.

r004.rationale: Says learning from the model’s own attempts can beat imitation of text, but does not say self-discovered solutions are better than others’ demonstrations because they reflect the model’s own way of solving.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between learning from what other people have written down and learning by actually trying to do things. In pre-training, you’re mostly reading the internet. That gives you an enormous amount of knowledge, but it doesn’t necessarily teach you how to work through a problem that takes days, notice when your approach is failing, and try something else.

Imagine a model learning to code. It can attempt a task, run the code, see which tests fail, and iterate. There’s a signal there that isn’t just, “Did you predict the next token correctly?” It’s, “Did your solution actually work?” And you can potentially generate a huge amount of that experience without needing a human to write out every example.

The hard part is making that process produce genuine progress. If the model is just generating text and then training on its own text, that’s not automatically new knowledge. You need feedback from something: a compiler, an experiment, an environment where success and failure mean something. And you need tasks that are difficult enough to teach it something but not so difficult that it never succeeds.

So the exciting possibility is a system that doesn’t just absorb the existing stock of human knowledge. It can practice, conduct experiments, and learn from the results. If you get that loop working reliably, the amount it can learn is much less constrained by how much useful text humans have already produced.

r001.rationale: Contrasts pre-training as mostly reading the internet with actively trying tasks, observing failures, and iterating.

r002.rationale: Does not compare in-context learning and pre-training sample efficiency.

r003.rationale: Does not describe reinforcement learning as distilling in-context learning into model weights.

r004.rationale: Mentions learning from the model’s own attempts, but does not say its self-discovered solutions are better training data than others’ demonstrations because they match its own problem-solving approach.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between learning from the work other people have already done and learning by doing work yourself. In pre-training, you’re reading the internet: you see the finished paper, you see the code somebody checked in. You don’t necessarily see all the failed experiments, the debugging, the process that produced that result.

Imagine instead that you give a model a programming problem. It tries an approach, runs the code, gets an error, figures out what went wrong, and tries again. There’s potentially a much richer learning signal there. And you can generate more of those experiences without waiting for humans to write more text.

The important caveat is that just having a model produce more tokens doesn’t accomplish this. If it’s generating answers and then treating its own answers as correct, it can reinforce its mistakes. You need some way of grounding the process: tests, an experiment, an outcome you can check. That’s why coding and math seem like natural places to start.

Then the question is whether you can turn those individual experiences into general improvements. Can the model learn a debugging strategy that helps on the next thousand problems, rather than just solve the problem in front of it? If you can do that reliably, you have a system that can keep acquiring capabilities through experience. Pre-training gives it a starting point, but human-written data no longer has to be the ceiling.

r001.rationale: It contrasts pre-training on finished papers and code with actively trying a problem, running code, debugging errors, and trying again.

r002.rationale: It says self-generated experiences can provide a richer learning signal, but does not state that in-context learning is more sample efficient than pre-training.

r003.rationale: It does not characterize reinforcement learning as distilling in-context learning into the model’s weights.

r004.rationale: It describes self-generated attempts as a richer signal, but does not say they are better because they reflect the model’s own way of solving problems.
